newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin said to back controversial telecoms deal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin said to back controversial telecoms deal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday approved his government's handling of a controversial telecommunications privatisation which has sparked a major public row in Russia.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, in televised remarks, said: "Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) is satisfied, above all, that the tender was conducted according to the strict rules which had been laid down and were observed."

He was speaking after briefing Yeltsin at his Volzhsky Utyos holiday residence in central Russia on last week's auction of a quarter stake in the telecommunications holding giant Svyazinvest, Russia's biggest privatisation.
The row has pitted reformist ministers against some of the country's most influential media, controlled by major banks, and Chubais made clear he wanted the war of words to end.
Chubais was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying Yeltsin had asked him to urge business circles to "give preference to calm business over emotions".
"Privatisation does not end with this deal," he said adding that in 1997 "we will have several major privatisation projects, including most profitable entities in the oil industry".
Several other big sales are coming up, including the Rosneft oil company and 38 percent of Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's biggest metals producers.
Deputy Prime Minister Alfred Kokh, who is in charge of privatisation, told reporters after the official signing of the Svyazinvest deal that the Norilsk sale may also be "emotional".

The public row flared up last weekend after it was announced that the Svyazinvest tender had been won by a consortium built around Uneximbank. The bank, Russia's third biggest, is headed by Vladimir Potanin, a first deputy prime minister until March.

It was backed by several foreign entities, including Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), the London-based investment banking division of Germany's Deutsche Bank, billionaire U.S. financier George Soros, and U.S. group Morgan Stanley Asset Management.
They offered $1.875 billion against $1.71 billion offered by the other bidder.
Chubais praised the price, much higher than the starting offer of $1.18 billion, saying this would cover half of the state's wage arrears in the public sector and the armed forces.
The success of the tender would attract investors from abroad and at home to future auctions. "The competition will get tougher and the price of the deals will go up," he was quoted as saying.

Participants in the losing consortium have not been officially named. But Potanin and the Russian media have said they were Vladimir Gusinsky, founder of the Most financial and industrial group, and tycoon Boris Berezovsky, who has formally dropped his business roles to take up a Kremlin post.

Powerful media organisations controlled by the two men's business groups have launched a bitter attack on the Svyazinvest deal, saying it was a shadowy affair between state officials and financial magnates. Chubais's fellow first deputy premier Boris Nemtsov came in for particular criticism.

Prominent ORT television presenter Sergei Dorenko opened the attack at the weekend and then told Kommersant newspaper on Tuesday he believed Nemtsov had acted incorrectly over Svyazinvest and said he was "twitching" like a "cockroach".
ORT is 51 percent state-owned, but Berezovsky's empire also has a major stake in the channel.
NTV television, part of Gusinsky's business empire, has accused unspecified bankers of using government contacts to build up funds to back a Nemstov bid for the presidency in the year 2000.
Ministers have denied any wrongdoing and Nemtsov called the media reaction "hysterical".
